1. In the graph I notice that the greater the scale meaning with guns involved, means a negative correlation of murder cases that were solved. The greatest percentages of murders cleared showed less percentages of gun use.

5. (thoughts after reveal)- I guess other variables affect the amount of solved murders as well, it also has to do with the city. Places with more crime means lots of cases to solve so more negative correlations. There's a lot that factors into this.

It shows that overall when there are more murders with guns, less murder cases are cleared. A catchy title would be, "more murders with guns, more cases left unsolved".
5. The reveal taught me that Gary, Indiana showed unusual data. It was very far from the trend line or averages. I didn't realize this until the reveal.

raw_comment:
1. This graph appears to show a correlation between a crime being committed with a gun and the likelihood of that crime being solved. From the graph we can see that a murders becomes less likely to be cleared as the likelihood of involvement of a gun increases. Another thing I noticed is that not every data point is labeled which I found to be a bit strange. 
2. I wonder if this is causation or just correlation. This could be interesting evidence showing that the more gun violence occurs the less justice is served (good title?) or maybe it shows the efficacy of the police force in these cities. I am not really sure but another thing that I wonder is how or why they chose these cities in particular. As I mentioned earlier, not every data point is labeled and I wonder if the cities are chosen by random, population or some other method. 
3.  Luckily Hawaii is not a place where violence is particularly common, especially gun violence. I believe that gun ownership hovers around 12-15% usually. Just out of interest with some quick research I put together a quick data point for Hawaii and found that in 2019 we had 32 homicides, 20 of which were solved giving us 62.5% of murders cleared. We had 62 gun related deaths in 2019 with around 66% being suicide and 23% being homicides (the other 11% probably being hunting related). Eventually we get 63% murders solved and about 43% of homicides with guns.https://efsgv.org/state/hawaii/https://projectcoldcase.org/cold-case-homicide-stats/

raw_comment:
My headline: Who pulled the trigger?

First of all, the FBI and police agencies' report emphasizes how crimes with guns increase/decrease the possibility of a crime being solved. These can be seen, for example, in New York, which has a lower percentage of crimes committed with guns (less than 60%) but with more than 80% of crimes solved. While in cities where there are more gun crimes, such as Gary, Ind., with more than 90% of murders with guns, they have less than 20% of murders cleared.

Now, what factors could be influencing the likelihood of a gun murder being solved or not? This New York Times article likely wants to point to the controversial issue of gun laws in the United States, with variations in each state and many hidden conflicts of interest.

One of the main consequences of the poor gun restrictions is the impossibility of knowing who has access to guns, who owns them, and even if that person is physically and psychologically able to own a firearm. However, just a few months ago, Texas approved buying and carrying a gun without a license. While many applauded the fact, this evidence of graphics and data ends up being terrible news for this region. Guns make it challenging to solve a crime.

Finally, we can only hope that the government and the different states can reevaluate the gun control laws and come up with a solution that seeks the general welfare, not the profit of the gun industry in the country.

raw_comment:
I notice that this graph shows the line of best fit for the relation of solved murders to the percentage of murders with guns. I noticed that very few of the cities are actually on the line, with many outliers. Perhaps the mean and line of best fit aren't the best measurement for this particular article.

I wonder which cities weren't included in this list, and what would happen if the measurement was extended to other nations, like the UK, Australia, France, China, Japan, India, South Africa, and Brazil.

My imaginary headline for this is "The Murder Weapon: Armed Murders in Relation to Murders Solved"

raw_comment:
What do you notice?

I noticed how the New York Times got to pick which cities they wanted to graph. This is not a scientific study, but a political opinion trying to make it look like a scientific study. They created a trend line where places with less guns have a higher solving rate. Places with more guns have a lower solving rate. 

What do you wonder?

What is the motive behind this graph? I doubt science is behind it or the truth. I wonder why they are being dishonest and not trying to find the truth or put in all the data points and names of the cities?

How does this relate to you and your community?

This does not relate to my community because it is not named on the graph. What does relate is how the New York Times is trying to sway public opinion into removing guns out of the community. I live in a low income neighborhood with a high crime rate. If the government creates restrictions with guns then criminals will have guns and law abiding citizens will not. 

What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.

"The lies behind the numbers...How the New York Times sways the public opinion against gun ownership."

raw_comment:
I noticed that there is a negative slope. In addition, the x axis starts at 50 making the graph a little misleading. There was a lot of cities in California which I thought was interesting.

I wonder if the guns were registered because I feel like that could factor in making the case harder to solve. Also, what type of gun was used because the murderer could have used a rare type or a commonly used type. Most importantly, if the investigators have the gun to even begin with because we don't know whether they actually had the murder weapon or just the bullet wound. I think all of these factors could affect the likelihood of solving the case. 

This relates to me and my community because it's important to take into consideration things like this when deciding to move somewhere. For example, I never want to live in Gary, Indiana. 

The graph is trying to show if there is a relationship between the percent of murders cleared that have guns involved. 
Catchy Headline: Homicide Gun Case With No Suspect in Place

raw_comment:
I noticed that there is a negative slope. In addition, the x axis starts at 50 making the graph a little misleading. There was a lot of cities in California which I thought was interesting.

I wonder if the guns were registered because I feel like that could factor in making the case harder to solve. Also, what type of gun was used because the murderer could have used a rare type or a commonly used type. Most importantly, if the investigators have the gun to even begin with because we don't know whether they actually had the murder weapon or just the bullet wound. I think all of these factors could affect the likelihood of solving the case. 

This relates to me and my community because it's important to take into consideration things like this when deciding to move somewhere. For example, I never want to live in Gary, Indiana. 

The graph is trying to show if there is a relationship between the percent of murders cleared that have guns involved.

raw_comment: After viewing this graph, there are many things that can be noticed. To start, in cities with a larger percentage of murders done with guns, not as many murders were solved as those done without guns. This leads me to believe that murders done with guns are harder to solve, which can make these cities much more dangerous than cities with murders done without guns. While looking at this graph, I wonder how many murders were committed in each city each year on the graph. This would allow me to be able to understand which cities are safer regardless of murders done with or without guns. I also wonder which cities on the graph have more gun control. This would help readers understand how gun control can affect the crime rate in different cities. This relates to me because I have always wondered how the ownership and use of guns can affect crime in different cities. This can relate to my community because in America, many different citizens continuously argue about the use of guns. This allows people to have a better understand of how they affect society when used in the wrong way. In this graph, we see how murders committed with guns affect there chance of being solved. A catchy headline for this graph could be "more murders done with guns means more criminals on the run".

raw_comment: In this graph, I notice that the likeliness of solving a murder that is involved with a gun is slim. I think this is because the type of combat that involves guns, in a sense, is not hand-to-hand combat. When people fire a gun it is something that is used from a distance. I wonder what kind of action the police force is taking because this is a problem. Innocent lives are being taken and the families of these victims don't even have the chance to know who caused their family pain. I also wonder what the government is doing about it. For the past few years now, the topic of gun restriction has been huge in America. Many groups of society believe that guns should be banned and I wonder if this topic of unsolved murders comes into the discussion. I also noticed that there are points on the graph that are not labeled and so I wonder what type of role they play in the graph. The town of Gary, Indiana has approximately 95% of murders that happen with guns. Out of this 95%, only about 5% were cleared. Maybe in smaller towns, it is harder to uncover crimes. This affects my community because I live only about 45 minutes from New York.  A catchy headline is "Who Can Solve the Case?"

raw_comment:
I noticed that the increase of gun usage decreased the percentage of cleared murder cases.

What I'm curious about is the fact that gunshot murder cases would be harder to solve, when it should be relatively easy to find fingerprints on them. Also, they are bulkier than knives or a few other types of weapons, which would have made them more noticeable and the murderer easier to catch. Not to mention, the echo of the gunshot in the surrounding areas.

My community in general is more or less peaceful, but this graph makes me wonder how many murders are taking place without guns, or the killer being caught. The data helps me be more aware of the dangers around me and causes me to think of more ways to avoid those situations.

The more murders that are caused by guns, the less those cases are solved.

Similarly, students who want to travel out of state for college would know what cities to avoid.

This applies to me and my community because I live in a very densely populated area and when there are a lot of crimes going on at once, it is very difficult to ensure protection and equal attention to every problem.

Thanks to all students who responded.   

Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received:  “Murder Cases with Guns: How Hard Can They Be?” by Yadira of Mesa, Arizona; “Can a Bullet Solve a Case or Will It Fly By?” by Luisana and "More Guns, Less Held Accountable" by Kenna both of Chico, California; "Getting Away with Gun Murder" by Everett of Gladeville Middle School, Mount Juliet, Tennessee; “Not Bullet Proof: Why Are So Many Gun Murders unsolved?” by Tessa of Andover, Massachusetts and "How Guns Can Impact Justice: Will You Ever Know the Killer?" by Valentine of Eleanor Roosevelt High School in New York City.

raw_comment:
I noticed that murders including guns are less likely to get solved.  Murders committed without guns are more likely to get solved than murders committed with guns.  This is because murders committed by guns can be done from far away.  Since gun murders can be done from far away, fingerprints of the murderer are less likely to be found.  I also noticed that there are many unnamed dots on the scatter plot.  These unnamed and named dots represent cities in the country. I wonder what cities the unnamed dots represent. I wonder what kind of murders make up the other part of the percentage.  What are the governments of states with low case solving percentages doing to try to solve more cases.  This affects my community because many lives have been lost in my community and the country.  It’s sad that many cases are unsolved.  Families of the murdered deserve to know what happened and to receive justice for their lost ones. This relates to me because solving murder cases can bring people justice in my nearby communities.

raw_comment: It does look like there may be an inverse relationship, but there is so much spread that it is hard to tell. This is partly because the population size is so big so that there is more room for variation. I think it's very interesting that the bigger counties are on the upper left hand of the graph. For example, Sacramento and New York, which have budgets of tens of billions of dollars. raw_comment:
What I have noticed is that the more cities that have gun-related murders, they went less cleared than the cities with more non-firearm murders. This could be from the fact that with a gun, a murderer would shoot and run off, while with another murder weapon, such as a knife, they would have to make contact with the victim, which their contact could be traced back to them. I wonder why gun-related murders go less unclear, despite the fact that gunshots can be heard from miles away. As a community, the best we can do is to be careful and let law enforcement deal with such issues, but gun control could be regulated better in these areas to lower murder rates and ensure that cases could be less likely to go unsolved. 
The Problems Firearms Possesses

raw_comment: In this graph, I notice how California has the most cities named out of any state on the graph. California also has all of its cities' murders cleared over 50% except for San Bernardino. I wonder if the accessibility of guns in each city and/or state affects the number of murders that occur. In this case, Clayton County, GA, has the most murders with guns which is not a city I would expect to have such a high rating. I also question if more urban cities have a higher murder-solve rate because there is a better chance of having valid witnesses in more populated cities. If this is true, that would mean finding murderers in rural cities is more difficult because there is much more land and way fewer people. This relates to me and my community because I can look at the towns closest to me on this graph and see the number of murders with guns and the percentage of those murders which were solved. This is extremely important in seeing the safety and security of a city as well as the success rate of their police. A headline for this graph that showcases what is going on would be, "Cities' Murder Rates with Guns and its Connection to Solving Cases."

raw_comment: In this graph it depicts the numbers of cases cleared versus the number of murders with guns. Sacramento County takes top place for the most murders solved. I can not help but wonder in this graph how often these murders happen in each state. If murders are less likely a police unit will have more time to solve a case versus if a unit gets a new murder everyday. In a place like Chicago, gun violence is extremely high that it may be so hard to solve everyone, bring them so far down on the list they aren't even worth listing. Being a high school senior, some of the college towns of the colleges I am applying too are on this list. It makes me feel a little unsafe but also gives me reassurance seeing how high many of the cases cleared are. An appropriate title could be "gun murders cleared and uncleared".

raw_comment: The first thing I noticed in the graph is that the percentage of murders compared to the percentage of murders cleared does not show a clear result of perhaps more murders committed with guns and a low percentage of murders cleared. raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's line moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph tries to answer the question whether it is easier or harder to solve murder cases if they were committed with guns.  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions plus, a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, Nov. 12 with moderation on Wednesday, Nov. 17.  The topic:  problematic holiday present deliveries.  Keep noticing and wondering.

raw_comment:
The first thing that I noticed about this graph was that Chicago is not listed. I know that Chicago has a large gun trafficking problem along with a high crime rate (mainly gun related), despite them having the strictest gun laws in the nation. Something I also noticed was that many of these cities are in the midwest or just not on the coastlines. I think this is because most of those cities are in states with little to no gun laws.

What I also wonder is why so many California cities are listed here. California has very strict gun laws, but most of the cities are below the trend line. Why is that?

This relates to me in my community because it displays that gun related crimes still occur frequently in places with strict gun laws, which tells me that either the law isn't enforced or just isn't working. 

Headline: Are gun crimes harder to solve?

Q1. California has many cities that show up on the graph. All of their cities but San Bernardino have over 50% murders cleared. For example, the shooting of Iremamber Sykap that occurred in April of this year, was a case where 16–year-old Iremamber was shot and killed through the rear view mirror of the car he stole at an intersection. This one made the news because even though we knew what had happened to some degree, the officers were not going to go to trial at first. Honolulu, where I reside in, is not a very gun crazy place, with an average of 37% of homicides involving a gun, however, when cases like this make it only the news, it does call attention to those in blue carrying guns. 
Q4. Is your city guncrazy or are they just happy to solve murders?

raw_comment: Something I noticed is that Chicago wasn't labeled on the graph. Chicago has some of the strictest gun laws in the nation, yet over 90% of murders in Chicago are gun murders. Chicago is almost on the trend line, with just under 60% of the murders solved. The graph demonstrates that gun murders are harder to solve, but ignores the far more important fact that gun control doesn't prevent gun violence. Someone might look at this graph and think, "In order to solve more cases, we need less gun murders, so we need less guns, and therefore we need stricter gun control." However, when you notice that cities like Chicago with strict gun laws still have high violent crime rates, it is apparent that stricter gun control is not the solution. One of the leading predictors of violent crime is rates of fatherless homes. Statistics show that in general, a 10 percent increase in fatherless kids results in a 17 percent increase in juvenile crime. Therefore, while the New York Times implies that less guns mean more solved crimes, and therefore safer cities, guns aren't the problem. The problems are societal. The question shouldn't be "What are the most common weapons in murders?", because people will always find another way to kill each other. The question should be "What can we as a society do to increase the numbers of fathers in homes?" We need to address why people commit murders, and not how.  It is more important to prevent murders than to solve them.

raw_comment:
I notice that there is a negative association between percent of murders solved and percent of murders with guns. The association is that the lower the percentage solved, the higher the gun percentage. I notice that New York has the highest percent of solved murders and the lowest percent of murders with guns. Gary, Indiana has the lowest percent of solved murders. Clayton County, Georgia has the highest percent of murders with guns, which is 100%.

I wonder if the correlation between murders solved and murders with guns means causation or not. If so, I wonder why the weapon being a gun makes the murder harder to solve. I wonder why one place has 100% of murders with guns, and I wonder why New York City has both the least gun murders and the most solved murders. I wonder if this graph was created to illustrate the problem of gun violence in the US.

Although none of the cities in the graph are in my state or adjacent states, violence and crime still affects everyone. Clearly gun control is a national issue.

“Do Guns Make Murders Harder To Solve?”

We notice that each point on the graph represents a city in the United States. We also noticed that there is a line of best fit, which means that the data is a scatter plot. The x axis is percent of murders with guns, and the y axis percent of murdered solved. Using this information, we inferred that the more crimes involve a gun, the less they are solved.
We see that New York has one of the highest percentages of solved murders. Knowing that New York has some of the strictest gun laws in the country, we wonder if these laws contribute to the higher percentage of solved crimes. Another thing we wonder is how accurate this line of best is, considering that the scatter plot points are pretty spread out. Similarly, we wonder if outliers on the graph like Gary Indiana affect the line of the best fit, and to what extent.
This is important for our community because it gives us an insight to the affects that higher gun access creates. While we are fortunate to live in a place like New York, it has opened our eyes to other places through this graph.
Finally, one catchy title could be: "Guns and Crime: America's new Epidemic"

I noticed that bigger states and places like New York and Los Angeles have more murders cleared when compared to smaller places like Dayton, Ohio. This surprises me, and makes me wonder why these bigger places with way more possibilities in a case have more cleared murders, than a smaller place like Dayton, Ohio, where there would be less more possibilities in a case. Adding on to this, I would think that solving a murder case in a much smaller place would be much easier than solving a murder case in a place like New York where it'd be much bigger and much more spread out.

raw_comment:
What do I notice: I notice that there is a strong negative correlation. Another thing that I notice is that as the murders with guns increases, the percent of murders cleared decreases. Lastly, I notice that a lot of the larger cities (New York, Los Angeles, Las Vegas) have a high percentage of murder cases dropped compared to other cities.

What do I wonder: I wonder what this would look like in the Midwest. There aren’t as many large cities compared to some of the other areas of the United States. Another thing I wonder is what are the number of cases in each of the cities and are the numbers really high for this type of crime. I also wonder what some of the other cities are that aren’t labeled in the graph.

How does this relate to me and my community: There has been an increase in gun violence around where I live. It isn’t a major city compared to the names on this graph. This has made me more aware of what is going on around me along with the nation.

Headline of the graph: How to get away with murder
